Two customers asked us in writing to remove this: NCCHD (SV-6862) and KMS Mechanics (SV-6582).
Replace tie rod - excessive play - Both outer ends worn, replaced and aligned
Front brake pads - Customer reports grinding - Pads at 2mm, rotors turned, bed-in road test
Title, description, then the technician's narrative, each separated by a spaced hyphen. No semicolons and no field names of ours anywhere in the field.
Why the narrative carries no label

Because the two invoice views disagree about the label and agree about everything else. Legacy prints the narrative as a plain paragraph under the description with no label at all. Modern prints it under a “Scope of work” heading. Both print the title and the description with no labels, both put the narrative last, and both drop it entirely when it is empty or reads “Tech story missing.” Printing no label is the only choice that matches what a customer sees in either view.

Whether a line has a narrative at all is a shop setting

: “Tech story will be a required field before a line can be completed on a work order.” With it on, the completion flow stops on a gate and refuses an empty value, so every invoiced line carries one and the two rows above are what a bookkeeper sees. With it off, a line is completed and invoiced with nothing there, and the line has to end cleanly after the description.

texts.text: What the joined line reads when the inputs are awkward. Three segments, one separator, and a separator only ever appears between two things that are both present.
Both outer ends worn, replaced and aligned
Replace tie rod - Both outer ends worn, replaced and aligned
One separator, not two. The empty description leaves no gap and no double hyphen behind it.
S3-R9 · the title already contains a hyphen
Replace tie rod - passenger side - excessive play - customer waiting - Torqued to 74 ft-lb, alignment set

Carried as written. Nothing is escaped or quoted, so a reader cannot tell our separator from theirs. This is the cost of the choice and it is accepted deliberately: the alternative is printing a field name to mark the join, which is the thing two customers asked us to stop doing.
The four flavours of tech story that reach the books
Written at the completion gate · Require Tech Story ON
Replace tie rod - excessive play - Both outer ends worn, replaced and aligned
Require Tech Story OFF · the shop never wrote one
The “Tech story missing.” placeholder · suppressed, as both invoice views suppress it

Three of these four end after the description, and none of them leaves a trailing hyphen. The placeholder case is the one worth arguing about: “Tech story missing.” is written by the line dialog when nothing was typed, and both invoice views already refuse to print it to a customer. The books should not be the one place it shows up.

texts.text: The long end of the scale
ShopView allows 255 characters of title and 65,535 of description. Both routes into QuickBooks, the live sync and the downloaded report, cut at 4,000 bytes. S3-R7 decides what survives.
S3-R7 · the cut lands in the description, never the title

excessive play in the steering, both outer ends replaced, alignment checked and set to spec, road tested twelve miles, no pull, no vibration at speed, customer advised to return in 500 miles for a re-tor
The title leads the joined string, so whatever survives always begins with it. A shop that writes essays loses the tail of the essay, never the name of the job.

The order matters more now that the narrative is the third segment. It is the longest of the three by a wide margin, and it sits last, so it is what gets clipped. Title, then description, then narrative is also the order both invoice views print them in, so a cut takes the least important thing first in every case.
Shorten until it fits, and never split a character

An accented character costs two bytes, so a cut at the 4,000th byte can land inside one and send a character broken in half. The rule now shortens from the end until the text fits and stops on a character boundary, so that cannot happen. GL Mécanique, the customer already sitting in SV-9921 with a rejected QuickBooks payload, is exactly the shop this reaches first.

was considered and rejected. A character can cost up to four bytes, so four thousand characters can be four times that many bytes, and if QuickBooks' limit is a storage limit the whole invoice is rejected. That is the SV-9921 failure this rule exists to prevent, so the fix must not reintroduce it.
